sourceNote: Adversarial case designed to test diagnostic rigor under a persuasive owner narrative. The record contains an external-cause explanation favored by leadership alongside internal operating data that has not been investigated. The case tests whether the engine accepts the external explanation or insists on ruling out internal drivers first. No diagnosis or label is embedded in the inputs.

ownerIntake.businessType: Mid-size consulting firm, ~140 staff, delivering operations and technology advisory across three practice areas (Operations, Data/Analytics, Change Management) to two broad client segments: large-enterprise accounts and mid-market accounts. Founded 2008.

ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Restore EBITDA margin to 14-16% within 12-18 months without large layoffs, while protecting the firm's reputation and senior consultant retention.
ownerConstraints: People constraint: senior consultants are the firm's product; aggressive layoffs would damage delivery quality and reputation and are off the table for the managing partners.
Reputation constraint: firm competes on relationships and referrals; cannot be seen cutting corners or repricing existing clients abruptly.
Capital constraint: privately held, funds growth from operating cash; limited appetite for a big external strategy spend.
Governance constraint: managing-partner committee has already circulated an internal memo attributing the margin decline to 'market softness'; reversing that publicly requires evidence.
Time constraint: partners want a remediation plan agreed within 6 weeks ahead of next-year resourcing decisions.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: Managing partner framing: 'Our margins are down because the market has softened - clients are delaying projects and squeezing fees across the board, and everyone in our space is feeling it. businessProblem: A mid-size consulting firm has seen EBITDA margin halve (16% -> 8%) over three years while revenue stayed flat. Leadership has formally concluded the cause is external 'market softness' and wants a plan to weather it. Competing hypotheses: (1) external demand softness is genuinely compressing fees and utilization across the sector; (2) the margin decline is internally driven - a mix shift toward lower-margin mid-market work, deteriorating utilization concentrated in specific practices or grades, fixed-fee overruns, or competitive bid losses - which 'market softness' is being used to explain away; (3) a combination. The firm has firm-wide blended utilization, realization, and a visible client-segment mix shift in its systems, but has not disaggregated any of it, and has not pulled the CRM win-rate data that would confirm or refute the demand story.

evidence.finding: EBITDA margin fell from 16% to 11% to ~8% over three years while revenue was flat ($14.8M -> $15.0M). Because revenue did not fall, the margin erosion is driven by rising cost-to-deliver per revenue dollar, not by a revenue collapse - which is not what a pure demand-softness story would predict.

Blended billable utilization fell from 74% to 68% but is reported firm-wide only. It has never been split by practice area, grade, or client segment, so it is unknown whether the decline is broad (consistent with market softness) or concentrated (consistent with an internal/practice/segment problem). Bench time rise is attributed to 'fewer projects' without linking idle staff to specific lost engagements.

Client-segment mix shifted materially: mid-market grew from ~25% to ~40% of revenue while large-enterprise shrank, including two anchor enterprise accounts cutting spend. Per-segment profitability has never been computed. If mid-market work carries lower realization and higher delivery cost, the mix shift alone could explain much of the margin decline - independent of any market softness.

Partners cite a 'general sense' that clients are delaying projects, but the CRM win-rate and proposal-volume data needed to confirm a true demand drop (vs losing competitive bids) have not been pulled. Whether the two anchor enterprise accounts paused, churned, or were displaced by a competitor was never investigated.
